The United States first realized the strategic importance of these remote islands at the outset of World War II, when Major General Simon Buckner Jr., tasked with the defense of Alaska, said the Aleutian chain “formed a spear pointing right at the heart of Japan.”1 The Japanese had already recognized this threat. Their reconnaissance of the Aleutians in the 1930s enabled successful carrier-based raids against Dutch Harbor and the occupation of Kiska and Attu in 1942. Japan thus prevented U.S. forces from using the islands as a staging point for a campaign against the Japanese mainland.
